extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in journalism/media studies conducting quantitative analyses (regression, commonality analysis) of influences on news content
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating how extramedia, organizational, and within-media variables predict reporters' perceptions of influences on news content using multiple regression, commonality analysis, and diagnostic screening. The rubric covers model selection, interpretation of coefficients, checking assumptions, and use of bootstrapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsimony in model selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the most parsimonious model that explains the largest amount of variance with the fewest number of variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a variable may not be essential for inclusion for parsimony, retain variables that are relevant because they contribute in conjunction with other variables. Consider removing predictors that make virtually no unique or joint contribution to produce a simpler model ("most parsimonious model includes only two independent variables—Economic and Owner/Executive Pressures").

rubrics_metrics.name: Report total variance explained (R2 and adjusted R2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the percentage of variation in the dependent variable explained by the regression model (R2 and adjusted R2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: full regression model explains 22% (or 22.6%, 47.2%, 55.4% etc.) of the variance; report adjusted R2 where appropriate (e.g., 47% adjusted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Present regression coefficients and inferential statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide unstandardized coefficients (B), standard errors (SE B), standardized beta weights (β), t-statistics, and p-levels for each predictor and the constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables should show B, SE B, β, t, and p (e.g., Table 4.9, Table 4.14). Use significance thresholds (e.g., p < .001, p < .010) to assess individual predictors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess unique contribution of each predictor via multiple regression
rubrics_metrics.description: After controlling for other variables, evaluate how well each predictor uniquely predicts the outcome (the unique contribution after partialing out others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use t-statistics and unique R2 contributions from commonality analysis to determine unique predictive strength (e.g., Owner/Executive Pressure makes a unique contribution of nearly 12%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commonality analysis to partition explained variance
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct a commonality analysis to decompose total R2 into portions unique to each predictor and portions common/shared among predictors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report figures representing R2 values for unique and common components (e.g., Unique to Adv = .167, Common to All = .029). Use the analysis to illustrate interrelationships and to identify which predictor is the biggest contributor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and interpret suppressor effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert for suppression when a predictor's standardized beta weight is negative while its correlation coefficient with the outcome is positive (or vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When suppression is present, note it explicitly (e.g., "it may be a suppressor variable"); consult literature (e.g., Tabachnick & Fidell) to interpret suppressor variables as enhancing the importance of other IVs by suppressing irrelevant variance. Report that there is no statistical means to precisely evaluate magnitude of suppression but discuss implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model comparison via reduced-variable regressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare full models and reduced (parsimonious) models by excluding non-contributing variables and evaluating changes in R2 and F-statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example approach: run a two-variable regression after excluding an insignificantly contributing third variable; report whether total variance explained remains similar and whether F-statistic increases (indicating improved model significance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use F-statistic for overall model significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the F-statistic and corresponding p-value to indicate whether the combination of predictors significantly predicts the dependent variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: F(3,608) = 181.504, p < .001; note changes in F when moving to reduced models (e.g., jump in F when excluding a suppressor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify strongest predictor by largest unique R2 / β
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the dominant predictor(s) by examining which predictor explains the largest portion of variance (largest unique R2) and/or has the largest standardized beta weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use commonality analysis to report percent variance explained by each predictor and unique contributions (e.g., Owner/Executive Pressure explains 37% with a unique 12%, Advertiser explains 21.4% with unique 17%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report regression equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Present final regression equations with coefficients for interpretation and potential replication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide equations for final models (e.g., Content Influence/Outcome = .503*Adv + .312*PR + .079*Political/Gov’t Official + 13.683).

rubrics_metrics.name: Check predictor intercorrelations and multicollinearity
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide correlation matrices showing interrelationships among predictors and between predictors and outcomes; assess whether intercorrelations are large enough to warrant multicollinearity concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present tables of correlations (e.g., Table 4.8, 4.13, 4.18) and state when "no relationship is large enough to warrant suspicion of multicollinearity." Consider variance inflation diagnostics if needed (not shown here but implied).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic screening of regression assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Screen residuals and other diagnostics to ensure regression assumptions are met (normality, homoscedasticity, independent errors, linearity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Karakostas's technique: (1) group predicted values into categories; (2) perform one-way ANOVA to test whether residual means are equal across categories; (3) run Levene's test to check equality of residual variances across categories. Check residual skewness and kurtosis and use Shapiro-Wilks for normality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address violations of assumptions with bootstrapping
rubrics_metrics.description: If residuals show non-normality or heteroscedasticity, re-evaluate analyses using bootstrapped samples to assess stability of parameter estimates and standard errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: re-run regressions with 2,000 bootstrapped samples; compare bootstrapped parameter estimates and SEs to original results and report whether differences are negligible; report final values based on actual data if bootstrapping confirms robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate sample size reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Always report sample size (n) for analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: n = 612 reported in tables and analyses; include degrees of freedom in F-statistics and t-tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse-code variables when necessary and document coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverse-code ordinal or scale variables where appropriate to ensure that higher values represent the intended direction (e.g., larger DMA ranks represent larger markets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state reverse-coding decisions and rationale to clarify interpretation of correlations and regression coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use control variables and test indirect/mediated paths
rubrics_metrics.description: Include control variables (e.g., Market Size) to test their direct and indirect effects on dependent variables; be open to exploratory re-specification if hypothesized direct effects are nonsignificant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a proposed direct effect is nonsignificant, examine whether the control variable operates indirectly via other constructs (e.g., Market Size affected Extramedia Influences, which then affected Organizational and Within-Media influences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report and interpret common/shared contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting commonality analysis, describe not only unique contributions but also the amount of variance common to pairs or all predictors and what that implies about joint influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: report percent "common to both" (e.g., 25% common to Owner/Exec & Econ) and explain how predictors partially achieve contributions in combination with each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis testing based on regression output
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept or reject hypotheses based on significance and strength of predictors as evidenced by t-tests, p-values, and unique contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hypothesis 8 accepted because Owner/Exec t = 11.775, p < .001 and unique contribution ~12%; Hypothesis 9 accepted because Advertiser t = 11.433, p < .001 and unique contribution ~17%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret negative regression weights carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: When a predictor has a negative regression weight but a positive correlation with the outcome, interpret cautiously as this may indicate suppression or net negative suppression rather than a substantive negative relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explanation and cite literature on suppression (e.g., Tabachnick & Fidell); do not automatically discard such variables—explain their role in enhancing other IVs by removing irrelevant variance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order effects in commonality and regression analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that entering independent variables in different orders can affect t-statistics and estimates in commonality analyses used to describe unique contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report that t-statistics for commonality analysis are from regression analyses in which independent variables were entered in different orders; may omit full tables for clarity but mention the method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document analytic decisions and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly document decisions (e.g., omitting tables for clarity, choice to report actual-data values after bootstrapping) and acknowledge strengths and limitations of chosen analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain rationale for methodological choices and note when supplemental outputs (e.g., bootstrapped vs. actual) are similar and thus actual data values are reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hierarchical/integrative theoretical framing for model building
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground variable selection and model structure in theoretical frameworks (e.g., Shoemaker and Reese hierarchical model of influences) and ensure model tests align with theory-driven hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame analyses around constructs like extramedia, organizational, and within-media influences and the outcomes (agenda building, frame building, agenda cutting); use theory to specify hypothesized direct/indirect relationships and control variables.
